title: Multiple Assignment
summary: Assign several variables in one line, swap values, and write values that span several lines.
intro: Python lets one line do the work of several. You will unpack many values at once, swap and rotate variables without a temporary variable, and spread long values across lines.

steps.title: Several names at once
steps.body:
Put several names on the left of `=` and the same number of values on the right, separated by commas. Python pairs them up in order. This is called *unpacking*, and it keeps related values together on one line.

```python
name, age, active = "Ana", 31, True
```

To give several names the same starting value, chain the `=` signs. This is *chained assignment*:

```python
wins = losses = 0
```

Each name is its own variable. Rebinding `wins` later leaves `losses` at `0`.

The counts must match exactly. Too many or too few values stops the program:

```python
# a, b = 1, 2, 3  # ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
# a, b, c = 1, 2  # ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 3, got 2)
```

example.title: City scoreboard
example.prompt: Unpack a city's details in one line, start two counters at zero, and print everything.
example.code:
city, population, country = "Lisbon", 545_000, "Portugal"
wins = losses = 0
print("City:", city)
print("Population:", population)
print("Country:", country)
print("Wins:", wins, "Losses:", losses)
wins = 3
print("Wins:", wins, "Losses:", losses)
example.output:
City: Lisbon
Population: 545000
Country: Portugal
Wins: 0 Losses: 0
Wins: 3 Losses: 0
example.explanation: The first line pairs `city`, `population`, and `country` with the three values in order. `wins = losses = 0` binds both names to `0`. Setting `wins = 3` rebinds only `wins`, so `losses` stays `0`.

practice.title: Movie votes
practice.prompt:
Store a movie's details in one line and track its votes.

1. Unpack `"Arrival"`, `2016`, and `7.9` into `title`, `year`, and `rating` in one line.
2. Set `likes` and `dislikes` to `0` with chained assignment.
3. Print `Title:`, `Year:`, and `Rating:` lines, each followed by its value.
4. Print `Likes:` with `likes`, then `Dislikes:` with `dislikes`, all on one line.
5. Set `likes` to `12` and print that votes line again.

Expected output:

```text
Title: Arrival
Year: 2016
Rating: 7.9
Likes: 0 Dislikes: 0
Likes: 12 Dislikes: 0
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: unpack "Arrival", 2016, and 7.9 into title, year, and rating in one line

# TODO: set likes and dislikes to 0 with chained assignment

# TODO: print the five lines shown in the prompt
practice.solution:
title, year, rating = "Arrival", 2016, 7.9
likes = dislikes = 0
print("Title:", title)
print("Year:", year)
print("Rating:", rating)
print("Likes:", likes, "Dislikes:", dislikes)
likes = 12
print("Likes:", likes, "Dislikes:", dislikes)

tests.output:
Title: Arrival
Year: 2016
Rating: 7.9
Likes: 0 Dislikes: 0
Likes: 12 Dislikes: 0

hints: Copy the shape of the example: three names on the left of `=`, three values on the right, in the same order.
Chained assignment writes both names and the value on one line, joined by `=` signs. Assigning `likes` again later changes only `likes`.

steps.title: Swapping values
steps.body:
Unpacking gives you the classic swap in one line, with no temporary variable:

```python
a, b = b, a
```

It works because Python evaluates the whole right side first, holding the old values of `b` and `a`. Only then does it assign them to the names on the left.

Two separate lines do not swap. The first line overwrites `a`, so its old value is lost:

```python
a = b  # a now holds b's value
b = a  # b gets its own value back, a's old value is gone
```

The same trick rotates three or more values. Each name on the left takes the value written below it on the right:

```python
x, y, z = y, z, x  # every value moves one place left
```

example.title: Swap and rotate colors
example.prompt: Swap two directions, then rotate three colors one place to the left.
example.code:
first, second = "left", "right"
print("Before:", first, second)
first, second = second, first
print("After:", first, second)

r, g, b = "red", "green", "blue"
print(r, g, b)
r, g, b = g, b, r
print(r, g, b)
example.output:
Before: left right
After: right left
red green blue
green blue red
example.explanation: In `first, second = second, first` the right side is read first as `"right", "left"`, then assigned. In `r, g, b = g, b, r` the old values are `"green", "blue", "red"`, so each color moves one place left.

practice.title: Podium and shifts
practice.prompt:
Swap the top two finishers, then rotate three work shifts the other way.

1. Swap `gold` and `silver` in one line, between the two prints.
2. Rotate `a`, `b`, and `c` in one line so `a` gets `c`'s value, `b` gets `a`'s, and `c` gets `b`'s.
3. Keep the given prints so the before and after values both show.

Expected output:

```text
Before: Maya Theo
After: Theo Maya
morning evening night
night morning evening
```
practice.starter:
gold, silver = "Maya", "Theo"
print("Before:", gold, silver)
# TODO: swap gold and silver in one line
print("After:", gold, silver)

a, b, c = "morning", "evening", "night"
print(a, b, c)
# TODO: rotate so a gets c's value, b gets a's, and c gets b's
print(a, b, c)
practice.solution:
gold, silver = "Maya", "Theo"
print("Before:", gold, silver)
gold, silver = silver, gold
print("After:", gold, silver)

a, b, c = "morning", "evening", "night"
print(a, b, c)
a, b, c = c, a, b
print(a, b, c)

tests.output:
Before: Maya Theo
After: Theo Maya
morning evening night
night morning evening

hints: Mirror the example's swap: the same two names on both sides of `=`, in opposite order.
For the rotation, keep `a, b, c` on the left. Under each name, write on the right the variable whose old value that name should get.

steps.title: Values that span lines
steps.body:
A string in triple quotes, `"""..."""`, can span several lines. Every newline you type becomes part of the string, so it prints exactly as written. Start the text right after the opening quotes, or the string begins with a newline and prints a blank line first. Likewise, put the closing quotes right after the last word, or the output ends with an extra blank line.

```python
note = """Line one
Line two"""
```

To split a long *line of code* without adding newlines, wrap it in parentheses. Python joins lines inside `()` automatically. Two string literals written next to each other are glued into one string, so a long text can sit on several lines:

```python
tip = (
    "Keep each piece short "
    "and end it with a space."
)
```

Watch the spaces: adjacent pieces are joined with nothing between them.

A backslash at the end of a line also continues it, but PEP 8 prefers parentheses. It is fragile: one invisible space after the `\` is a SyntaxError (unexpected character after line continuation character).

```python
tip = "Keep each piece short " \
    "and end it with a space."  # works, but avoid it
```

example.title: Poem and message
example.prompt: Print a three-line poem from one triple-quoted string, then a long message built from two pieces.
example.code:
poem = """Roses are red,
Violets are blue,
Python is fun."""
print(poem)

message = (
    "Short lessons and quick practice "
    "help you learn a little every day."
)
print(message)
example.output:
Roses are red,
Violets are blue,
Python is fun.
Short lessons and quick practice help you learn a little every day.
example.explanation: The triple-quoted string keeps both line breaks, so one `print()` writes three lines. Inside the parentheses the two literals are joined into one string. The space at the end of the first piece keeps `practice` and `help` apart.

practice.title: Address label
practice.prompt:
Print an address label and a long tip built from shorter pieces.

1. Assign the three label lines (`Ada Lovelace`, `12 Byron Street`, `London`) to `label` with one triple-quoted string, then print it.
2. Build `sentence` inside parentheses from two adjacent string literals on two lines: `"Read the example first, "` and `"then solve the practice in a few minutes."`. Then print it.

Expected output:

```text
Ada Lovelace
12 Byron Street
London
Read the example first, then solve the practice in a few minutes.
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: assign the three-line address label to label with triple quotes, then print it

# TODO: build sentence from two adjacent strings inside parentheses, then print it
practice.solution:
label = """Ada Lovelace
12 Byron Street
London"""
print(label)

sentence = (
    "Read the example first, "
    "then solve the practice in a few minutes."
)
print(sentence)

tests.output:
Ada Lovelace
12 Byron Street
London
Read the example first, then solve the practice in a few minutes.

hints: Start the label text right after the opening `"""` so there is no blank first line.
Put the two strings on their own lines inside `(` and `)` with nothing between them.

recap:
- `a, b, c = 1, 2, 3` unpacks values into names in order, and the counts must match.
- `x = y = 0` gives several names the same value.
- `a, b = b, a` swaps because the right side is evaluated first.
- `a, b, c = b, c, a` rotates three values in one line.
- Triple-quoted strings keep their line breaks.
- Inside parentheses a line can continue, and adjacent string literals join into one.
